newsitem.title: UK: UK unions urged to avoid "industrial warfare".
newsitem.headline: UK unions urged to avoid "industrial warfare".

text.p: Britain's Trades Union Congress (TUC) urged its members on Monday not to try to use the election of a Labour government to wage "industrial warfare" against employers.

TUC general secretary John Monks told a conference of union leaders that they should instead avoid strikes where possible and seek a constructive "social partnership" with employers and the government.
"Some on our side may think a changed political climate will help us in some kind of industrial warfare -- that way lies disaster," Monks said. "The mature way is the partnership way."

Unions, whose powers were considerably eroded by anti-union legislation during the last 18 years of Conservative rule, would again enjoy greater influence if they were seen to be improving industrial relations, Monks added.
"Frankly, the more we can avoid industrial action, the higher will be our public standing."
TUC membership has dwindled to below seven million from a 1970s peak of 13 million due to the decline of heavy industry, low recruitment in services and anti-union legislation.
Opinion polls suggest the opposition Labour party, under its centrist leader Tony Blair, will defeat Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives in an election due by May 22.
Blair has tried to distance Labour from the union movement from which the party originally sprang, but unions still wield considerable influence and remain major contributors to party funds.
Monks said the Conservatives were likely to try to frighten voters by reminding them that the last two Labour governments had ended amid widespread industrial unrest.
"Those memories are potent, especially with older voters, and we can expect the desperate Tories to stir them in the election campaign," he said.
To shake off these "tired images," unions had to become part of the solution to problems such as unemployment and low investment.

Acknowledging the fears of some trade unionists that Labour has moved too far to the right under Blair, Monks nevertheless insisted that there were key difference between Labour and the Conservatives.
Labour would introduce a national minimum wage, sign up to the European Union's Social Chapter on workers' rights and introduce statutory rights to union recognition, he said.

But Monks also noted that the modern Labour party was "not all convinced that a close continuous involvement with the TUC or its own affiliated unions is essential or advantageous, especially if that involvement leads to strikes and discords."
